prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Richard, King, Let

outputs.L1:
*(From* Richard II, *spoken by King Richard)*

No matter where; of comfort no man speak.  
Let’s talk of graves, of worms, and epitaphs;  
Make dust our paper, and with rainy eyes  
Write sorrow on the bosom of the earth.  
Let’s choose executors and talk of wills—  
And yet not so, for what can we bequeath  
Save our deposed bodies to the ground?  
Our lands, our lives, and all are Bolingbroke’s,  
And nothing can we call our own but death  
And that small model of the barren earth  
Which serves as paste and cover to our bones.

For God’s sake, let us sit upon the ground  
And tell sad stories of the death of kings:  
How some have been deposed; some slain in war;  
Some haunted by the ghosts they have deposed;  
Some poisoned by their wives; some sleeping killed—  
All murdered. For within the hollow crown  
That rounds the mortal temples of a king  
Keeps Death his court, and there the antic sits,  
Scoffing his state and grinning at his pomp;  
Allowing him a breath, a little scene,  
To monarchize, be feared, and kill with looks;  
Infusing him with self and vain conceit,  
As if this flesh, which walls about our life,  
Were brass impregnable; and, humored thus,  
Comes at the last and, with a little pin,  
Bores through his castle wall—and farewell, king!

Cover your heads, and mock not flesh and blood  
With solemn reverence. Throw away respect,  
Tradition, form, and ceremonious duty,  
For you have but mistook me all this while.  
I live with bread like you, feel want,  
Taste grief, need friends. Subjected thus,  
How can you say to me, I am a king?
outputs.L2:
It does not matter where we go—let no one offer consolation. Instead, let us speak of burial places, decay, and the words carved on tombs. Let the dust become our page, and with tear-filled eyes inscribe our grief upon the earth. We might appoint executors and discuss our wills—yet what is left for us to give away except our dethroned bodies to the soil? Bolingbroke possesses our estates, our lives, and everything else. Only death remains ours, along with this little form of lifeless clay that encloses and covers our bones.

For God’s sake, let us sit on the ground and recount mournful tales about how kings have died: some stripped of their thrones, some killed in battle, some tormented by the spirits of rulers they themselves overthrew, some poisoned by their wives, and others murdered in their sleep. Every one of them has been slain. Within the empty crown encircling a king’s mortal head, Death holds court like a jester, laughing at royal authority and sneering at its magnificence. For a short while, Death permits the ruler to play his part—to reign, inspire fear, and seem capable of killing with a mere glance. He fills the king with pride and persuades him that the flesh surrounding his life is an invulnerable wall of brass. After indulging that illusion, Death arrives with a tiny pin, pierces the fortress, and the king is finished.

Cover your heads. Do not insult ordinary flesh and blood by treating me with solemn reverence. Cast aside deference, custom, ceremony, and formal obligation, because all this time you have misunderstood what I am. Like you, I survive by eating bread; I suffer deprivation, experience sorrow, and need companions. Since I am subject to the same human frailties, how can you still call me a king?
outputs.L3:
Richard rejects all comfort and turns his thoughts instead toward graves, death, and sorrow. Having been deposed by Bolingbroke, he feels stripped of everything that once defined his kingship. Nothing remains truly his, he believes, except his own body and the death that will eventually claim it.

This loss leads Richard to reflect on the fate of kings more generally. However powerful or exalted they may appear, rulers cannot escape mortality and often meet violent or tragic ends. Death, he imagines, hides within the hollow crown, mocking royal ceremony and grandeur while waiting to destroy the fragile human body beneath them. The symbols of monarchy may make a king seem exceptional, but they offer no protection against suffering or death.

Richard therefore casts aside the rituals and illusions of kingship. He insists that he is fundamentally no different from any other person: he needs food to survive, feels pain, experiences grief, and depends on the companionship and support of friends. In this moment, his fall from power exposes the ordinary, vulnerable human being concealed beneath the royal title.
outputs.L4:
Facing the prospect of deposition, King Richard II rejects the consolation offered by his followers and turns instead to a bleak meditation on mortality. He asks them to sit upon the ground and tell sad stories of the deaths of kings. Some monarchs, he reflects, have been deposed, others killed in battle, poisoned by their wives, or murdered in their sleep. Although kings surround themselves with ceremony and appear powerful, history shows that they remain subject to betrayal, suffering, and death.

Richard develops this idea through images of graves, wills, and inheritance. A king may possess lands and command a nation, yet in death he requires only a small piece of earth for a grave. His royal titles cannot preserve his body, and his authority cannot prevent his possessions from passing to others. The legal and ceremonial structures associated with monarchy—crowns, estates, succession, and royal commands—therefore seem insignificant when measured against human mortality.

At the center of Richard’s meditation is the image of Death enthroned within the hollow crown. Death hides inside the symbol of royal authority, mocking the ruler who wears it. For a time, the king is allowed to act as though he were invulnerable: he commands subjects, receives homage, and believes that his body is protected by sacred status. Yet this illusion ends when Death pierces the “castle wall” of his flesh. The crown may suggest divine power and permanence, but it rests upon a fragile human head.

Richard’s speech strips kingship of its grandeur and exposes the vulnerable person beneath the royal role. He asks his companions to abandon formal respect and recognize that he, too, needs food, feels grief, and depends upon friends. In this moment, he understands that ceremony cannot transform mortal flesh into something immortal. Beneath the pomp of monarchy, a king is merely a human being—afraid, wounded, and destined to die like everyone else.
outputs.L5:
### Richard the King

Richard was a king known for his courage, ambition, and skill in battle. Although he spent much of his reign far from England, stories of his bravery made him a legendary figure. His supporters admired him as Richard the Lionheart, while his critics questioned whether a king should remain so distant from his kingdom.

“Let my actions speak for me,” Richard might have said as he prepared for another campaign. Yet leadership requires more than military strength. A successful king must also protect his people, maintain peace, and govern with wisdom. Richard’s life reminds us that heroism and good leadership are not always the same.
